en: The *Huayan Cailin* (Forest of Aids for the Avataṃsaka), composed by the National Teacher Xianshou of the Right Tang:
Regarding the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*, their meanings are manifold; yet when one investigates its definitive teaching, it comprehensively elucidates cause and effect.
There are two gates:
the cause is the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra,
and the fruit is the karmic activity of Vairocana.
These various realms constitute the essence,
while dependent origination constitutes the function;
thus, both essence and function are fully encompassed.
Perfectly pervasive and uniform throughout,
when one speaks of its underlying cause,
it does not go beyond dependent origination.
Turning through the meaning,
one melts through and masters both existence and emptiness;
following the function of the mirror of wisdom.
It expounds many gates according to the profound essence of its principle;
it expounds a single meaning according to that very essence.
If one discusses the profound purport,
neither "one" nor "many" is applicable; yet,
by not taking "one" as the realization of oneness, nor "many" as the realization of multiplicity, [the truth is revealed].
It is eternally existent, eternally empty, and eternally present;
such is the grand significance.
This is a brief and general outline.
Now, focusing on the essential meaning,
I shall briefly set forth a dialogue; however,
I will merely state the general outline.
The remainder belongs to the scriptural text;
it is hoped that gentlemen seeking the Way will explore its underlying significance.

1. An inquiry into the Universal Eye; 2. Clarifying principle and phenomena; 3. Distinguishing the true cause; 4. Harmonizing the Great and Small Vehicles; 5. Concluding on formation and destruction; 6. Penetrating the two realms; 7. Clarifying concealment and manifestation; 8. Clarifying cause and effect; 9. Reaching the realization that form and emptiness are one. An Inquiry into the Universal Eye: An inquiry concerning the mutual dependence of the eye and form.
There must indeed be such a thing;
the principle of the conjunction between the sense faculties and their objects is not non-existent.
When conditions converge and manifest, how can one avoid encountering objects?
And in what way is it called the "Universal Eye"? I replied: Five conditions serve as the cause.
The eye is designated as the fruit.
If it manifests through conditions,
then those very conditions are designated as the "eye."
If the cause were to be subsumed within the effect such that all conditions were designated as "eye," then the entirety of visible form would constitute the eye.
It is constantly seeing yet lacks an object;
the entire eye constitutes form.
It is always called "seeing," yet it is not the self.
It is not that I am devoid of feeling or thought; rather,
being without objective conditions, I have severed all craving and seeking,
gathering the myriad phenomena before my very eyes.
The entirety of the ten directions lies within the range of the eye;
thus, because the meaning of conditions is inexhaustible,
one perceives them as they appear without reaching a final limit.
The nature of things is difficult to perceive through thought;
one must accord with the phenomena as they are, for they are difficult to standardize.
When the ten dharmas are established, the eye is universal and its meaning is pervasive.
Thus one sees that the entire body has long been self-concealed;
as concealment and illumination unfold, they become ever more layered.
Yet, one investigates the ten directions within the very limits of one's vision.
The mirror is empty yet luminous;
it gathers the myriad phenomena to form its body,
manifesting principle and phenomena with complete penetration.
I respectfully respond.
Second, clarifying principle and phenomena: the question concerns the phenomenal characteristics of dependent origination;
their respective boundaries are clearly delineated.
The rational nature of the dharma-realm has no location;
it is one and the same whether in existence or destruction.
The essence and its function are not distinct;
they also penetrate both phenomena and principle,
being gathered together as non-dual.
To eliminate these defects and clarify the profound essence of the school,
I have recorded here, as a private correspondence,
the origins and the phenomena of this matter.
Only by gathering back the nature can it be perfected;
likewise, the profound mystery of the Dharma-realm manifests emptiness in dependence upon conditions.
There is mutual interpenetration of existence;
essence and function are mysteriously pervasive.
To speak of phenomena is immediately to penetrate the source of emptiness.
Discourse on existence is but the penetration of emptiness beyond existence;
at times both are simultaneously stripped away,
such that not even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization remains.
At times they are mutually established;
the discourse on their vastness is seen together,
wherein the phenomena of total inclusion and the phenomena of total negation are taken as the principle.
Phenomena are not separate from reality;
things possess principle and thereby constitute phenomena.
In what direction could emptiness possibly follow after existence? As principle is realized, phenomena manifest accordingly.
When one contemplates from the perspective of ultimate unity,
the myriad things can be brought to a state of certainty.
This is my respectful reply.
3. Distinguishing the True Cause (Tṛtīyaṃ hetu-viniścaya). Question:
At this time, when entering the practice of the path, one must necessarily see the Buddha and seek the Dharma, proceeding from cause to fruit.
The box and its lid depend upon one another;
if one perceives the thirty-two marks as the cause,
then there is ultimately no mark to be seen.
If you take "emptiness alone" as the cause,
I fear that later on the principle and the phenomenon will become vastly separated;
I request that you distinguish the Buddha's cause.
I humbly pray to hear of the fruit of attaining Buddhahood. In private,
I have learned that the Buddha takes non-arising, emptiness, and quiescence as his body,
and likewise takes the non-origination of the dharma-realm as his essence.
One merely realizes this principle;
the Buddha manifests his body in accordance with this principle,
yet remains solely within the unborn.
The Dharma manifests its characteristics in accordance with wisdom;
yet these characteristics are themselves signless.
Thus, it is not unreasonable that the form-body (rūpakāya) is insufficient [to exhaustively represent the Buddha].
If it were non-existent, it would not be non-existent.
How could the gate of emptiness be considered substantial?
It has long been detached from silence and stillness.
That which has not been scrutinized throughout the three periods of time should already have transcended form and sound;
it is rarely encountered by the six sense organs.
Thereafter, one realizes the mind within;
by illuminating the principle, one attains Buddhahood,
which likewise consists in bringing external conditions to rest.
Wisdom proceeds toward the Dharma in the same manner as the practice;
when the cause is fulfilled, it is itself the fruit.
Once the resolve for enlightenment has been generated, the foundation for attaining perfect awakening is established.
When the fruit is fulfilled, the cause is thereby accomplished.
Attaining the Way originates from the very foundation of the initial resolve;
why must one wait until the cause has fully reached its fruition?
Fearing that this might give rise to a discourse on the nature of existence regarding the fundamental principles of the complete and partial aspects of phenomena,
I respectfully respond.
Fourth, the Integration of the Great and Small: Question—There are the Great and the Small, their characteristics clearly distinct;
one is expansive and the other is narrow.
Regarding the differentiation of phenomena:
if one attempts to subsume the great within the small,
there is a fear that the great may lose its original form.
If one attempts to encompass the small with the great,
there is also fear that the small will be injured for lack of substance;
thus, the broad and the narrow are inherently unequal.
How could the coming and going [of delusion] coexist?
The obscuring clouds are blocked;
this sun of wisdom shines brilliantly, facing me in private.
The great must encompass the small to be called "great," and the small must contain the great to receive the designation "small";
each lacks inherent nature.
It is because the large and the small can mutually contain one another that they do not ultimately reach completion;
it is by means of this that the broad and the narrow are equally admitted.
Thus we know that the great is the small and the great,
and the small is the large and the small;
the small has no fixed nature.
In the end, it pervades the ten directions of its own accord;
the Great is not a fixed form.
Spanning kalpas, it remains as radiant as a single lifetime.
Thus one knows that when the small is truly great, a mustard seed is contained within Mount Sumeru;
when the great is truly small,
the waters of the ocean are contained within a single pore.
If their respective natures were not destroyed,
how could their entering and exiting not be complete?
Furthermore, because they all retain their original forms.
Expanding and contracting spontaneously without obstruction.
I respectfully respond.
Regarding the five fetters and their formation and destruction: a question on the meaning of formation and destruction.
Although its principles are clear,
the various schools present them differently,
thereby deviating from their true intent.
At the time of formation, where does destruction reside?
At the time of destruction, in what direction does formation exist?
If these were different from the noble [reality], they could not be accommodated.
If you are the same as ordinary people and furthermore do not believe me,
please bring pearls and jade to serve as recompense;
I shall remove these shards and rubble in private response.
Destruction itself constitutes the locus of destruction;
it is also destruction that constitutes the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
It is empty and yet eternally existent.
Existence and destruction are thus thoroughly penetrated by emptiness and destruction;
substantial existence is thus revealed as emptiness within the realm of existence.
Thereafter, difference is neither different nor identical.
The essence is inherently luminous;
delusion is inherently obscure.
If one uses the rectitude of this nature to bind oneself to the two extremes of existence and emptiness.
If one uses wisdom to illuminate and penetrate the coming and going of arising and ceasing as being of a single limit, I respectfully respond.
Regarding the question of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) within the two realms: are sentient beings deluded?
The Buddhas have awakened to this;
although their essence is one,
there are differences according to their functions.
If one were to equate sentient beings with Buddhas,
then all Buddhas would be identical to delusion;
if one were to equate Buddhas with sentient beings, [the same confusion would follow].
May all sentient beings attain awakening together;
may they hope to wipe the mirror of their minds to reveal its great brilliance,
and thus strive to open the profound gateway.
Opening it as a dark chamber, Sidi replied:
"I have always taken those who are not sentient beings to be sentient beings,
and likewise taken those who are not Buddhas to be Buddhas."
Without obstruction, it remains while constantly being sublated;
without hindrance, it is destroyed while always being established.
Following conditions, it fully establishes the name "sentient beings."
How could there be any sentient beings to be found?
It is only by way of provisional designation regarding their essential nature that they are given the name "Dharmakāya.
How, indeed, could there be any Buddhas to be sought?
There is nothing that does not falsely penetrate the true source;
while abiding in the single characteristic, it is eternally present.
The True encompasses the false extremities.
Entering the five paths while remaining eternally empty;
when the mind encompasses all, the two realms are difficult to penetrate, yet through the teaching of wisdom they are easily explained as being one and the same.
Thereafter, the dual negation and dual affirmation mutually establish one another.
One perceives all Buddhas within the bodies of sentient beings and views sentient beings within the essence of the Buddha.
Regarding the sevenfold manifestation and concealment, one asks about the meaning of this manifestation and concealment.
Its profound intent is difficult to fathom;
it penetrates the mysterious by relying on emptiness and form,
and reveals the esoteric through the principles of unity and multiplicity.
If there were concealment during the time of manifestation,
then upon observing form, one would see emptiness;
if there were manifestation during the time of concealment, [the same would follow].
Seeing stillness, one should constantly observe movement.
I request that you open the treasury of the Dharma.
This jewel of wisdom—[I] respond in private.
This "ability to subsume" refers to this very thing being called "that.
If one includes this,
it is precisely this that reveals the hidden nature of that.
That which is hidden is precisely that which is manifest;
the time of manifestation is itself the time of concealment.
In a single destruction, they are entirely subsumed.
This manifest aspect is largely established,
while that hidden aspect is fully subsumed;
thus, the essence of phenomena remains eternally luminous.
Clarity is not manifestation;
the Buddha moves yet is eternally tranquil.
Tranquility is not concealment.
The hidden is established by means of the manifest;
the dharma-realm is opened up within dependent origination.
The manifest is accomplished by means of the hidden.
The myriad phenomena are mirrored within the single void;
yet to see the void is to see form,
and to comprehend the delusive is to comprehend the real.
How could it take eighty thousand [kalpas] to reach the pinnacle of body and mind?
This is my respectful reply.
8. Clarifying Cause and Effect. Question: Cause and effect are mutually dependent, like a box and its lid.
If one obtains the fruit from the cause...
If the fruit were identical to the cause at the time [of its arising],
then sentient beings would be identical to the stage of Buddhahood.
It cannot be called the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*), for this would again fall into the error of permanence (*śāśvata*).
I hope Your Reverence will guide me who am lost in the wrong direction and open this path of correctness. I replied privately:
The two stages of cause and effect are a single dependent origination;
they are established through mutual dependence.
Meaning does not arise in isolation;
it penetrates from the fruit to the source and exhausts the cause from its root to its branches.
Only when the practices and vows of Samantabhadra are fulfilled can they be called the perfect cause;
[only then] does the ten-fold body of Vairocana manifest.
Thus it is called the "fulfilled fruit.
Now, phenomena have no before or after;
rather, the cause is perfected according to the point at which realization occurs.
Although the Buddha has severed both permanence and annihilation,
when the time for awakening arrives, the principle manifests;
yet these successive fruits are not something to be attained.
The cause likewise does not perish;
it is only through the arousal of the mind that the fruit is verified,
for the fruit exhausts the limits of the cause.
Once the Bodhisattva has attained perfect enlightenment,
he immediately realizes that by comparing the causal source with the resultant stage,
one incurs the errors of nihilism and eternalism.
The single understanding of the same substance further gives rise to the consciousness of essence and function;
this can naturally be understood within the context of the gate of dependent origination.

It is granted that the characteristics of cause and effect are identical; yet, regarding the locus of realization within the *dharmadhātu*, the distinction between cause and fruit has already been discussed.
Through the ninefold penetration of form and emptiness, one inquires into the matters of dependent origination.
Regarding the distinction of boundaries:
the principle of the emptiness of the dharma-realm is free from all limitations.
The principle of "one penetrating and one obstructing" would be contradicted;
whether hidden or manifest,
there would be no standard for their harmonious integration.
I desire that our strength be equalized, that the meaning of the single flavor be revealed, and that we share the same source.
I hope to hear your virtuous voice;
I pray you will open your lofty song for my private audience.
Form is constituted by grasping emptiness,
just as moving waves gather water;
phenomena contain principle, and thus they are realized.
Like a golden vessel, this follows its form;
color is established in dependence upon space,
and space is clarified in relation to color.
If they mutually exclude one another, both meanings will necessarily perish;
if they mutually establish one another, both gates will manifest together,
such that when one appears, the other is simultaneously concealed.
Therefore, when observing form, it is always empty;
at the time of emptiness, form is immediately revealed.
Thus, when observing emptiness, it is constantly form.
Form is not form,
and emptiness is not emptiness;
they possess power in relation to one another, yet are mutually non-existent.
They mutually establish one another and mutually negate one another;
thus, the meaning of non-arising is fully revealed through their mutual establishment.
Thus, the gateway of dependent origination manifests:
form has no intrinsic nature;
its entire substance is utterly empty.
Emptiness has no self-nature;
emptiness fully encompasses form.
Form and emptiness are non-dual.
Perfectly pervasive and uniform throughout,
yet further allowing for one part to be unobstructed and another obstructed;
though it is universally present within all forms, it remains unfused.
There is a hidden understanding within the nature that is precisely centered.
I respectfully respond.
*Kegon Sakurin* concludes here. At this time, the fifth month of the Rabbit year in the twenty-fourth year of Meiji.
While studying at Nanshan,
I retrieved this book from the precious storehouse of the Śākyamuni Hall;
it happened that I received urgent news of my mother’s illness, as her four elements were in disharmony.
Desiring to go directly down the mountain to attend to the illness,
he prayed for a swift recovery to the Triple Gem and completed this writing immediately.
By the humble servant of Tōshōdai-ji Temple in Nanto.
The 17th day of the fifth month; requested by the śramaṇa Zhīhǎi, five years since his full ordination.
